# ToolMind Technical Report: A Large-Scale, Reasoning-Enhanced Tool-Use Dataset

Chen Yang Affiliation: Nanbeige Lab, BOSS Zhipin     Ran Le
Affiliation: Nanbeige Lab, BOSS Zhipin     Yun Xing

University of China {yangchen02, leran, songyang}@kanzhun.com, 
batmanfly@gmail.com    Yang Song ^(†)^(†)thanks: Corresponding author.

###### Abstract

Large Language Model (LLM) agents have developed rapidly in recent years
to solve complex real-world problems using external tools. However, the
scarcity of high-quality trajectories still hinders the development of
stronger LLM agents. Most existing works on multi-turn dialogue
synthesis validate correctness only at the trajectory level, which may
overlook turn-level errors that can propagate during training and
degrade model performance. To address these limitations, we introduce
ToolMind, a large-scale, high-quality tool-agentic dataset with 160k
synthetic data instances generated using over 20k tools and 200k
augmented open-source data instances. Our data synthesis pipeline first
constructs a function graph based on parameter correlations and then
uses a multi-agent framework to simulate realistic user–assistant–tool
interactions. Beyond trajectory-level validation, we employ fine-grained
turn-level filtering to remove erroneous or suboptimal steps, ensuring
that only high-quality reasoning traces are retained. This approach
mitigates error amplification during training while preserving
self-corrective reasoning signals essential for robust tool-use
learning. Models fine-tuned on ToolMind show significant improvements
over baselines on $`\tau`$-bench, $`\tau^{2}`$-bench, and BFCL-v4. The
dataset is available at
[https://huggingface.co/datasets/Nanbeige/ToolMind](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Nanbeige/ToolMind).

![Refer to caption](2511.15718v2/figures/toolmind_performance.png)

Figure 1: Performance on BFCL-v4, $`\tau`$-bench, and
$`\tau^{2}`$-bench.

## 1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have adopted Function Calling (FC) paradigm
to interact with external environments, significantly expanding their
capacity to solve complex real-world tasks [Zhao et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib22); [Qu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib23). This capability
hinges on the model’s proficiency in tool use, which requires reliable
interpretation of user instructions, appropriate function selection, and
precise parameter generation. A data-centric approach has proven
effective in enhancing such capabilities, typically requiring
large-scale, high-quality datasets with diverse and accurate
function-call demonstrations.

Recent studies have actively synthesized data for various function
calling scenarios [Liu et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib3); [Xi et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib4), spanning diverse application domains and interaction
modalities such as selection from large toolsets, parallel function
calls, and rejection of unspecified requests [Liu et al. ()](#bib.bib5);
[Prabhakar et al. (2025)](#bib.bib6); [Xu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib13).
However, existing datasets have several critical limitations: limited
scale, the absence of explicit reasoning traces, a lack of multi-turn
interactions, and insufficient query diversity. These issues highlights
the importance of high-quality, large-scale datasets to develop robust
and generalizable tool-use models and agents.

A key challenge in constructing high-quality datasets lies in capturing
the dynamic nature of real-world user–assistant interactions. First,
user requests are often under-specified, lacking sufficient parameters
for task completion (e.g., a query like “What’s the weather in Beijing?”
does not specify a time frame). Second, effective interaction requires
an ongoing clarification process, in which the assistant can proactively
request missing information from the user. Current open-source synthetic
datasets rarely capture these dynamics, leading to models struggling
with such scenarios.

In this work, we introduce ToolMind, a reasoning-enhanced tool-use
dataset comprising 360k samples. It integrates 160k assistant response
turns synthesized through multi-agent simulations and 200k augmented
turns adapted from open-source data. To ensure diversity, we collect 20k
functions from open-source datasets and construct a function graph that
captures inter-parameter correlations. Function chains are then sampled
via random walks on this graph to synthesize user intents. Then, we
employ a multi-agent framework for dialogue generation, orchestrating
three dedicated roles—user, agent, and tool—each instantiated by a
language model to capture the dynamics and complexities of real-world
tool-use interactions. Finally, we apply a rigorous two-stage filtering
process, comprising both trajectory-level and turn-level quality checks,
to ensure that all training samples contain only valid conversation
turns.

Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the ToolMind dataset in
enhancing the tool-use capabilities of LLMs. With supervised
fine-tuning (SFT), models of various scales show significant
improvements over baselines across multiple benchmarks, including
BFCL-v4 [Patil et al. ()](#bib.bib12), $`\tau`$-bench [Yao et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib7), and $`\tau^{2}`$-bench [Barres et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib14). Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  High-Quality Tool-Use Dataset. We introduce ToolMind, a large-scale,
  high-quality tool-use dataset comprising 360k samples that effectively
  addresses the key limitations of existing datasets—namely in scale,
  reasoning traces, multi-turn interactions, and query diversity.
- •
  Data Synthesis and Quality Filtering Pipeline. We develop a novel data
  synthesis pipeline that constructs a function graph based on parameter
  correlations and employs multi-agent simulations with three dedicated
  roles (a user, an assistant, and a tool), which better capture the
  dynamic nature of real-world tool-use interactions. A rigorous
  two-stage filtering process is further applied to ensure high data
  quality.
- •
  Effectiveness of Large-Scale Simulation. We show that ToolMind
  delivers significant and consistent performance improvements across
  models of various scales. These results empirically validate that
  large-scale synthetic data generated from simulated environments can
  serve as an effective alternative to real-world data for achieving
  substantial gains in model performance.

## 2 Background

Function Calling. The integration of external tools and functions into
language model workflows marks a major step toward extending model
capabilities beyond text generation. Function calling refers to the
structured mechanism through which language models invoke predefined
functions or APIs to access real-time data or interact with external
systems [Qu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib23). An early paradigm for using
external tools is React [Yao et al. (2022)](#bib.bib21), where models
generate both reasoning traces and corresponding function calls in an
interleaved manner. This paradigm was later refined and integrated into
thinking models as a native capability (_e.g.,_ supporting function
calling in chat templates) for training and inference [Yang et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib18); [Zeng et al. (2025)](#bib.bib24), also known as the
model’s function call pattern. Our synthetic data aims to enhance the
model’s native function calling capabilities.

Benchmarks. Several benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate the
tool-use ability of language models, _i.e.,_ their capacity to call
appropriate functions for task completion [Liu et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib1); [Qin et al. (2023)](#bib.bib2); [Guo et al.
(2025b)](#bib.bib11); [Patil et al. ()](#bib.bib12); [Yao et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib7); [Barres et al. (2025)](#bib.bib14); [Zhong et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib8). These benchmarks have evolved from basic tool-use
evaluations to assessing agent behavior in more realistic, interactive
scenarios. BFCL-v4 [Patil et al. ()](#bib.bib12) comprises four distinct
versions that systematically progress from single-turn interactions to
multi-turn dialogues, and from simple, static tool-use cases to complex
tasks involving search and memory capabilities. Concurrently,
$`\tau`$-bench [Yao et al. (2024)](#bib.bib7) focuses on sustained
dialogue and function-calling tasks and $`\tau^{2}`$-bench [Barres et
al. (2025)](#bib.bib14) further enriches this scenario by extending
function access to the user side. Together, these advances demonstrate a
clear shift toward more dynamic and complex evaluation frameworks that
better reflect real-world conditions. In this work, we evaluate models
across the three benchmarks mentioned above to systematically assess the
effectiveness of our synthesized data.

## 3 Methodology

In this section, we present our data synthesis pipeline, including graph
construction and function-chain sampling, multi-agent, multi-turn
trajectory synthesis, and two-stage quality filtering. The overall
synthesis pipeline is illustrated in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ ToolMind Technical Report: A Large-Scale, Reasoning-Enhanced Tool-Use Dataset").
All prompts used for trajectory synthesis and quality filtering are
provided in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Prompts ‣ ToolMind Technical Report: A Large-Scale, Reasoning-Enhanced Tool-Use Dataset").

![Refer to caption](2511.15718v2/ToolMind.png)

Figure 2: An illustration of the proposed data synthesis pipeline, with
three key components: (1) Graph Construction and Function Chain
Sampling, including function collection and refinement, function-graph
construction, and random-walk sampling; (2) Multi-Agent Multi-Turn
Trajectory Synthesis, using language models to simulate multiple roles
and generate interactive trajectories; and (3) Quality Filtering,
applying both trajectory-level and turn-level filtering to ensure data
quality.

### 3.1 Graph Construction and Function Chain Sampling.

We construct a directed graph over the collected functions to model
their input–output compatibility, and then sample function chains via
random walks for trajectory synthesis.

#### 3.1.1 Functions Collection and Preprocessing

Existing open-source works have already achieved substantial tool
diversity. Building on these resources, we collect functions from public
datasets—including xlam-function-calling-60k¹¹ 1
[https://huggingface.co/datasets/Salesforce/xlam-function-calling-60k](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Salesforce/xlam-function-calling-60k)
, glaive-function-calling-v2²² 2
[https://huggingface.co/datasets/glaiveai/glaive-function-calling-v2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/glaiveai/glaive-function-calling-v2)
, and ToolACE³³ 3
[https://huggingface.co/datasets/Team-ACE/ToolACE](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Team-ACE/ToolACE).
The resulting function set covers a broad range of function types,
complexity levels, and application domains, spanning everyday utilities
to domain-specific APIs. We denote the collected function set by
$`\mathcal{F}=\{f_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}`$, where each function $`f_{i}`$ has
an input space $`\mathcal{X}_{i}`$ and an output space
$`\mathcal{Y}_{i}`$, and may take multiple arguments, written as:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
f_{i}:\;\mathcal{X}_{i}\to\mathcal{Y}_{i},\qquad\mathcal{X}_{i}=\prod_{k=1}^{m_{i}}{x}_{i,k},\;\;\mathcal{Y}_{i}=\prod_{\ell=1}^{n_{i}}{y}_{i,\ell}.
``` |  |

To make these function sets compatible for downstream processing, we
first standardize incomplete or ambiguous functions (*e.g.,* those
missing explicit definitions in certain input or output parameters). We
use a language model to infer the missing descriptions and types for
each parameter $`r\in\mathcal{X}_{i}\cup\mathcal{Y}_{i}`$, denoted as
$`\mathrm{desc}(r)`$ and $`\mathrm{type}(r)`$. Once the specifications
are complete, we embed each parameter using a unified scheme. For each
$`r\in\mathcal{X}_{i}\cup\mathcal{Y}_{i}`$, we concatenate its
description and type with literal tags and encode them with an embedding
model:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{v}(r)=\phi\big(\text{{DESC}}\ \|\ \mathrm{desc}(r)\ \|\ \text{{TYPE}}\ \|\ \mathrm{type}(r)\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.
``` |  |

#### 3.1.2 Random Walk with Function Graph

With the parameter embeddings in place, we proceed to build a function
graph that captures relationships between functions. In this graph, each
function is a node, and edges are established based on the semantic fit
between outputs and inputs. Concretely, let $`G=(V,E)`$ be a directed
graph with $`V=\mathcal{F}`$. For two distinct functions $`f_{i}`$ and
$`f_{j}`$, we measure how well an output of $`f_{i}`$ can serve as an
input to $`f_{j}`$ by the maximum cosine similarity over their parameter
embeddings:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
s_{ij}\;=\;\max_{\,y\in\mathcal{Y}_{i},\;x\in\mathcal{X}_{j}}\operatorname{sim}\!\big(\mathbf{v}(y),\,\mathbf{v}(x)\big),
``` |  |

where $`\mathrm{sim}`$ denotes cosine similarity. An edge $`i\!\to\!j`$
is created when this similarity exceeds a fixed threshold $`\tau>0`$,
indicating that an output parameter of $`f_{i}`$ is semantically similar
to an input parameter of $`f_{j}`$. To ensure the reliability of these
connections, we further employ a language model as a validator and keep
only the accepted links.

We also introduce randomness into edge construction. This yields a more
diverse connectivity pattern that better reflects the real-world
function composition. With the constructed graph, we sample function
chains via random walks that traverse existing edges:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{W}=(f_{0},f_{1},\dots,f_{L}),L\sim\mathrm{Uniform}\{5,\dots,20\},
``` |  |

where $`\mathcal{W}`$ is a function chain, $`f_{t}`$ denotes the
function visited at step $`t`$, and $`L`$ is the walking length. To
avoid oversampling specific nodes, we impose a per-node visit limit
during the random walk process. This encourages balanced graph coverage
and mitigates bias toward high-degree hubs.

### 3.2 Multi-Agent Multi-Turn Trajectory Synthesis

Based on the sampled function chains, we synthesize user intents to
represent realistic user goals. A user intent represents the underlying
goal that a user aims to achieve, rather than the exact query they pose.
This distinction provides greater flexibility in modeling user behavior,
as users often express the same intent in diverse ways. Since the tools
are not executable in our setup, we employ a simulation framework to
generate responses. The trajectories are created through a multi-agent
simulation that involves three distinct agents:

- •
  User Agent: Initiates the interaction by asking questions based on
  synthesized intent and drives the conversation forward.
- •
  Assistant Agent: Responds to the user’s queries, provides guidance,
  asks for clarification, or calls external functions when needed.
- •
  Tool Agent: Simulates the execution of a function invoked by the
  assistant, returning tool responses based on simulated outputs.

These three agents operate in an iterative loop: the user agent poses a
query, the assistant agent responds, and the tool agent simulates
feedback when required. The process continues until a predefined turn
limit or stopping condition is reached. This simulation produces a
diverse set of interaction trajectories that serve as training data for
modeling rich user–assistant–tool dynamics.

Empirical results demonstrate that even without real-world interaction,
the large-scale synthetic data generated from these simulations
significantly improves model performance. The flexibility and diversity
of the simulated conversations provide valuable insights for training
models in complex, multi-agent systems. For a detailed example of the
generated data, see
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Examples ‣ ToolMind Technical Report: A Large-Scale, Reasoning-Enhanced Tool-Use Dataset").

### 3.3 Quality Filtering

To ensure that the synthesized interactions provide reliable learning
signals, we apply a two-stage quality filtering process:
trajectory-level filtering that maintains goal alignment and coherence,
followed by turn-level filtering that removes erroneous or misaligned
steps.

#### 3.3.1 Trajectory-Level Filtering

Given the predefined user intents (defined in the previous section), the
user agent first judges whether the task is completed or not during the
process of multi-turn interaction. Then, a second LLM evaluates goal
coverage, coherence, and cross-turn relevance. Only trajectories that
both align with the intent and exhibit a coherent flow are retained,
while the rest are discarded. This stage produces a high-quality pool of
trajectories for finer-grained filtering.

#### 3.3.2 Turn-Level Filtering

Since trajectory-level filtering operates at a coarse granularity, it
cannot effectively isolate erroneous turns within otherwise coherent
trajectories. Trajectories may still contain erroneous or misaligned
turns—such as failed intermediate attempts, tool calls based on
incorrect assumptions, or role drift in user/tool messages. To further
improve data quality, we address these remaining issues by applying a
separate LLM-based judge to each turn. The model then masks invalid or
role-inconsistent steps and retains only correct procedural actions,
ensuring the final training data targets effective problem solving and
precise tool use.

### 3.4 Data Statistics

![Refer to caption](2511.15718v2/figures/combined_analysis.png)

Figure 3: A distribution analysis of the proposed synthetic dataset.

We split each trajectory into multiple samples using the turns that
passed the turn-level quality filter and analyze both *trajectories*
(orange) and *post-split samples* (blue). See the distribution analysis
in
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.4 Data Statistics ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ ToolMind Technical Report: A Large-Scale, Reasoning-Enhanced Tool-Use Dataset").
From a trajectory-level perspective, the overall distribution of data
lengths is relatively uniform, and users show strong participation
throughout the dialogues. After the conversations are segmented into
turns and filters are applied, the distribution skews toward shorter
instances, which is expected. We further analyze the distribution of
step counts for consecutive tool calls. A sizable fraction of turns
proceed without any tool calls, likely because the synthetic user is
prompted to mimic natural dialogue—holding back some constraints so that
the model must ask follow-up questions and confirm details. Taken
together, these findings indicate that current tasks leave room for
greater complexity, motivating future work on more demanding tool-use
scenarios.

![Refer to caption](2511.15718v2/figures/domain_pie.png)

Figure 4: Distribution of user intent domains, with tail ($`\leq 2\%`$)
grouped as “others”.

In addition, we perform domain classification and statistical analysis
of user intents throughout the synthesis process. Because each intent is
composed via a function chain, a single intent can have multiple domain
labels. As
Figure [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.4 Data Statistics ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ ToolMind Technical Report: A Large-Scale, Reasoning-Enhanced Tool-Use Dataset")
shows, the data analysis and entertainment domains are the most
prevalent, while the remaining domains are relatively balanced.

## 4 Experiments

This section presents the performance of models of varying sizes after
supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on our dataset. We first present the
fine-tuning setup and then evaluate the resulting models against the
baselines on widely-used tool-calling benchmarks.

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

Model and Fine-tuning Setup. We perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on
Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-14B [Yang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib18). The training
is conducted using OpenRLHF [Hu et al. (2024)](#bib.bib15) framework
with a sequence length of 64k, a global batch size of 64, a learning
rate of 5e-6, and a warmup ratio of 0.03.

Benchmarks. We evaluate our models on three widely used tool-calling
benchmarks: BFCL-v4 [Patil et al. ()](#bib.bib12), $`\tau`$-Bench [Yao
et al. (2024)](#bib.bib7), and $`\tau^{2}`$-bench [Barres et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib14). For BFCL-v4, we use the official evaluation setup
for Qwen3 and benchmark our model against larger-scale models on the
official leaderboards as of October 2025. For a comprehensive
comparison, we incorporat results from both open-source models
DeepSeek-V3 [Liu et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib16), DeepSeek-R1-0528 [Guo et
al. (2025a)](#bib.bib17), Qwen3-235-instruct [Yang et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib18), Kimi-K2-Instruct [Team et al. (2025)](#bib.bib19)
and closed-source models GPT-4o-2024-11-20, GPT5-2025-0807, and
Gemini2.5-Pro [Comanici et al. (2025)](#bib.bib20). For $`\tau`$-Bench
and $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench, we used GPT-4o as a user simulator and evaluate
performance by directly comparing the model before and after
fine-tuning.

Datasets. The entire ToolMind dataset comprises two components: (i)
synthesized trajectories described in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Methodology ‣ ToolMind Technical Report: A Large-Scale, Reasoning-Enhanced Tool-Use Dataset")
and (ii) data augmented from open-source corpora. We incorporat the
following open-source datasets: xlam-function-calling-60k [Liu et al.
()](#bib.bib5), When2Call [Ross et al. (2025)](#bib.bib9),
glaive-function-calling-v2 ⁴⁴ 4
https://huggingface.co/datasets/glaiveai/glaive-function-calling-v2,
ToolACE [Liu et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib3), BUTTONInstruct [Chen et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib10), APIGen-MT-5k [Prabhakar et al. (2025)](#bib.bib6),
and the Tau-bench training set [Yao et al. (2024)](#bib.bib7). All
open-source multi-turn datasets are subjected to the same split and
quality-filtering procedures as the synthesised data. The statistics of
the datasets can be found in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ToolMind Technical Report: A Large-Scale, Reasoning-Enhanced Tool-Use Dataset").
After preprocessing, each multi-turn conversation is split at each
assistant message into multiple samples. For each splitted sample, we
retain the full prior context up to (and including) the anchor assistant
message and discard all subsequent turns. Each asisstant response is
structured into three parts: think, content, and tool calls. During
training, we compute loss only on the tokens of the anchored assistant
response.

On BFCL-v4, we observe notable improvements in both Qwen3-8B and
Qwen3-14B after training. Although their single-turn evaluation scores
show modest fluctuations, they remain above most baseline models.
Performance gains are most pronounced in multi-turn and agentic
evaluations. Notably, after training on ToolMind, Qwen3-14B surpasses
several larger-scale open-source and closed-source models. Similarly, on
the $`\tau`$-bench and $`\tau^{2}`$-bench benchmarks, both Qwen3-8B and
Qwen3-14B achieve substantial improvements in their average score after
training on ToolMind. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the
ToolMind dataset in improving model tool-use capabilities.

| Qwen3-8b (FC) | 35.83 | 35.65 | 36.00 | 34.64 | 43.86 | 32.00 | 28.07 | 42.21 |
|    with (a) synthesized data | 42.31 | 42.61 | 42.00 | 38.85 | 42.98 | 42.00 | 31.58 | 46.87 |
|    with (b) no turn-level filtering | 35.31 | 42.61 | 28.00 | 41.73 | 47.37 | 48.00 | 29.82 | 44.11 |
|    with (c) augmented open-source data | 48.65 | 51.30 | 46.00 | 42.16 | 57.89 | 44.00 | 24.56 | 45.88 |
|    with ToolMind | 46.70 | 57.39 | 36.00 | 46.41 | 59.65 | 48.00 | 31.58 | 46.92 |

Table 4: Ablation Study of ToolMind Components. Models trained on three
data configurations are compared: (a) synthesized data only, (b)
synthesized data without turn-level quality filtering, and (c) data
augmented from open-source datasets.

Ablation Study. To evaluate the effectiveness of each component in
ToolMind, we conduct an ablation study on Qwen3-8B. The study comprises
the following configurations: (a) using only synthesized data, (b) using
synthesized data without turn-level quality filtering, and (c) using
only data augmented from open-source datasets. The experimental results,
shown in
Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ToolMind Technical Report: A Large-Scale, Reasoning-Enhanced Tool-Use Dataset"),
demonstrate that the open-source augmented data contribute to
significant performance improvements on $`\tau`$-bench and
$`\tau^{2}`$-bench, while the graph sampling-based synthetic data lead
to major gains on BFCL-v4, and the turn-level quality filtering
significantly enhances the model performance. Moreover, the model
trained on the combined dataset achieves the best results across nearly
all evaluation metrics, demonstrating that each component of ToolMind is
integral and effective.

## 5 Conclusion

This paper presents ToolMind, a large-scale dataset designed to address
data scarcity in tool-use for Large Language Models. Built through
graph-based function sampling and multi-agent trajectory synthesis,
ToolMind offers diverse, realistic function-calling trajectories with
explicit reasoning traces. Experimental results demonstrate that models
fine-tuned on ToolMind achieve consistent and significant improvements
across multiple benchmarks. Our work highlights the value of
high-quality synthetic data for advancing tool-use capabilities and
provides a valuable resource for future research.
````
